prompt: What performance does a 100 GiB gp3 volume get without paying for any extra?
hint: It is the same at any size.

choices.text: 300 IOPS, three per GiB, and the throughput that allows
choices.why: That is gp2, where performance grows only with size.

choices.text: 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s, whatever the size of the volume
choices.why: Right. Anything above is a separate line on the bill.

choices.text: Whatever the instance type allows, with no limit of its own
choices.why: The volume has its own limits, and the instance has others on top.

choices.text: Only the storage; every IOPS is bought separately
choices.why: That is closer to io2. gp3 includes a baseline.

prompt: A gp3 volume of 200 GB is raised to 5,000 IOPS and left at 125 MiB/s. At 0.152 USD per GB-month and 0.0095 per IOPS-month above 3,000, what does it cost a month, in USD?
hint: Storage, plus the IOPS above the included 3,000.

prompt: A database needs 3,000 IOPS on 100 GiB of data. Why is gp3 the better choice than gp2?

choices.text: gp2 cannot be attached to current instance types
choices.why: It can; it is older, not withdrawn.

choices.text: gp2 would need 1,000 GiB to reach 3,000 IOPS, and gp3 includes them at any size
choices.why: Right. On gp2 the only lever is size.

choices.text: gp3 is a hard disk, and hard disks are faster for databases
choices.why: gp3 is SSD; the hard-disk types are st1 and sc1, and they are poor at random IOPS.

choices.text: gp2 has no IOPS limit, which makes it unpredictable
choices.why: It has one: three per GiB.

prompt: moto created a 100 GiB gp3 volume with 90,000 IOPS. What does AWS do with the same request?
hint: A ratio of IOPS to size.

choices.text: Creates it and caps the IOPS at the instance's limit
choices.why: The volume limit is checked when it is created, before any instance.

choices.text: Creates it, and bills the IOPS that are used
choices.why: Provisioned IOPS are billed whether used or not, and this many are refused anyway.

choices.text: Turns it into io2, which allows that rate
choices.why: AWS never changes the type you asked for.

choices.text: Refuses it: gp3 allows at most 500 IOPS per GiB
choices.why: Right, so 100 GiB stops at 50,000.

prompt: A gp3 volume provisioned at 250 MiB/s is attached to an m7i.large. What does the extra throughput buy?

choices.text: All of it, sustained, since the volume was provisioned for it
choices.why: The instance is a limit of its own, whatever the volume can do.

choices.text: Nothing, because gp3 throughput only applies to io2 instances
choices.why: io2 is a volume type, not an instance type.

choices.text: Double, because two volumes share the instance's bandwidth
choices.why: Sharing divides the bandwidth; it never doubles it.

choices.text: Bursts only: the instance sustains 81.25 MB/s to EBS
choices.why: Right. Size the instance and the volume together.

prompt: Which of these are true of an st1 volume? Choose all that apply.
hint: It is a hard disk sold for throughput.

choices.text: It cannot be a boot volume
choices.why: Neither hard-disk type can.

choices.text: AWS sells it from 125 GiB upwards
choices.why: moto accepted 10 GiB; AWS refuses it.

choices.text: It suits large sequential reads such as logs
choices.why: Throughput grows with its size.

choices.text: It is fast at small random reads
choices.why: That is where a hard disk is weakest.

choices.text: It includes 3,000 IOPS at any size
choices.why: That is gp3.

prompt: What does AWS answer to attaching a volume in sa-east-1b to an instance in sa-east-1a?

choices.text: It attaches it, more slowly, across the zones
choices.why: That is moto's answer, without the slowness. AWS never attaches across zones.

choices.text: It moves the volume into sa-east-1a, then attaches it
choices.why: A volume never leaves its zone; moving means a snapshot and a new volume.

choices.text: It refuses: InvalidVolume.ZoneMismatch
choices.why: Right. A volume attaches only within its zone.

choices.text: It attaches it read-only
choices.why: EBS has no such mode for a cross-zone attachment; it refuses.

prompt: Put the steps of growing an in-use XFS data volume from 100 to 200 GiB in order.
hint: The volume first, then what is inside it.
items: Run modify-volume with the new size
Wait until the modification reaches optimizing or completed
Grow the file system with xfs_growfs
trap: Growing the file system before the partition, or before the volume, finds no space to grow into.

prompt: An instance is terminated. A data volume attached to it after launch, with the default flag, is now what?
hint: DeleteOnTermination defaults to false for those.

choices.text: Available: unattached, intact, and still billed every month
choices.why: Right. Nobody is warned that it is still there.

choices.text: Deleted with the instance, like the root
choices.why: Only volumes whose flag is true go; the root's is, this one's is not.

choices.text: Attached to the next instance launched in the zone
choices.why: Nothing attaches a volume on its own.

choices.text: Turned into a snapshot automatically, and then deleted
choices.why: No snapshot is taken unless somebody takes one.

prompt: An account finds 12 forgotten gp3 volumes of 100 GB in the available state. At 0.152 USD per GB-month, what do they cost a month, in USD?
A volume attached to an instance after it was launched has DeleteOnTermination set to ___ unless somebody changes it.
hint: The root is the other value.

prompt: A scratch volume means nothing without its instance and should not outlive it. What is the right fix?
hint: The flag can be changed on a running instance.

choices.text: A weekly job that deletes every available volume
choices.why: It would also delete the data volumes somebody kept on purpose.

choices.text: Make it an instance store volume with modify-volume
choices.why: modify-volume changes size, type and performance among EBS types; instance store comes with the type.

choices.text: Detach it before every termination
choices.why: A detached volume survives just the same, and is still billed.

choices.text: Set its DeleteOnTermination to true
choices.why: Right, or in the launch template's mapping for a whole fleet.

prompt: An i4i.large is stopped and started again. What is on its 468 GB NVMe disk?

choices.text: Everything that was there before the stop
choices.why: That is a reboot, which stays on the same host.

choices.text: The data, restored from an automatic snapshot
choices.why: Instance store cannot be snapshotted at all.

choices.text: The data, read-only until the next reboot
choices.why: There is no data left to read.

choices.text: Nothing: it starts empty, on a new host
choices.why: Right. The old disk stayed with the old host and was erased.

prompt: Which of these belongs on instance store?

choices.text: The only copy of a PostgreSQL database
choices.why: A stop or a host failure takes it with no way back.

choices.text: Photos users uploaded
choices.why: Nobody can upload them again for you.

choices.text: A build cache whose originals are kept in S3
choices.why: Right. Losing it costs a refill and nothing else.

choices.text: The application's configuration, edited by hand
choices.why: A hand edit on a disk that vanishes is lost with it.

prompt: Three i4i.large (0.274 USD an hour) replace three r7i.large (0.21105) of the same vCPU and memory. How much more do they cost in a month of 730 hours, in USD?
hint: The difference per hour, times 730, times three.

prompt: Match each event to what it does to an instance store disk and to an EBS volume.

pairs.right: Instance store erased, EBS by its flag
Instance store lost, EBS kept in its zone

prompt: How many mount targets can one EFS file system have in one Availability Zone?

choices.text: One
choices.why: Right; a second gives MountTargetConflict.

choices.text: Two, one for each subnet type
choices.why: One per zone, in whichever subnet you choose.

choices.text: As many as the zone has subnets
choices.why: The second in the same zone is refused.

choices.text: None, since EFS is reached without one
choices.why: Instances reach it only through a target in their zone.

prompt: A mount target is reached over NFS on TCP port ___, which its security group has to allow.
A file system stores 60 GB in EFS Standard, at 0.57 USD per GB-month. What does it cost a month, in USD?
A team wants to put a PostgreSQL data directory on EFS, so that any instance can take over. Why is that a poor fit?

choices.text: Every operation crosses the network to a regional service, and a database is built around fast local I/O
choices.why: Right. Put the database on EBS, or use a managed database.

choices.text: EFS cannot store files larger than 1 GB
choices.why: File size is not the problem; latency is.

choices.text: EFS is only reachable from one zone
choices.why: It is reachable from every zone with a mount target.

choices.text: PostgreSQL refuses to start on encrypted storage
choices.why: Encryption is invisible to the database.

prompt: A file system was created without encryption. How is it made encrypted at rest?

choices.text: Turn encryption on with update-file-system
choices.why: Encryption at rest cannot be switched on later.

choices.text: Mount it with the tls option, which encrypts what is written
choices.why: tls encrypts the traffic on the way, not the stored files.

choices.text: A new one, encrypted from birth, plus a copy
choices.why: Right. The choice is made at creation.

choices.text: Add a KMS key to its mount targets
choices.why: Mount targets are network interfaces; they hold no key.

prompt: Which of these belong on EFS? Choose all that apply.
hint: Files several machines read and write.

choices.text: Uploads shared by four web servers in three zones
choices.why: The case EFS exists for.

choices.text: Users' home directories on a fleet of machines
choices.why: Every machine sees the same files.

choices.text: The data directory of a busy MySQL
choices.why: Network latency on every operation; EBS fits.

choices.text: A dataset that many workers read
choices.why: One copy, read from every zone.

choices.text: An instance's root volume
choices.why: An instance boots from EBS, not from a network file system.

prompt: Four web servers in three zones must all see the same uploaded files, which nobody can recreate. Where do the files go?

choices.text: A large gp3 volume attached to all four
choices.why: A volume attaches to instances in one zone, and is not a shared file system.

choices.text: EFS, with a mount target in each of the three zones
choices.why: Right. Each server mounts the target in its own zone.

choices.text: The instance store of the largest server
choices.why: It vanishes with a stop, and the other three cannot reach it.

choices.text: A gp3 volume per server, synchronised by a nightly snapshot
choices.why: Four copies a day apart are four different sets of files.

prompt: Order these from the cheapest per GB-month on the price sheet to the dearest.
trap: Per gigabyte is not per month: EFS bills what is stored and a volume what is provisioned.

prompt: A Kafka cluster keeps every partition on three brokers, each an i4i.large writing to its instance store. One broker's host fails. What happens to its data?
hint: Lost on that host, kept elsewhere.

choices.text: AWS restores it from the instance store's backup
choices.why: There is no backup of instance store.

choices.text: It is gone for good, and the cluster loses those partitions
choices.why: Two other brokers hold each partition.

choices.text: A new broker refills from the other two
choices.why: Right. Replication is what makes instance store safe here.

choices.text: The disk moves with the instance to a new host
choices.why: An instance store disk stays with the host it belongs to.
